title: Taxes on Inheritance Money: Federal Rules, State Taxes and Inherited IRAs
summary: An inheritance generally isn’t taxable on its own, but what you inherit and where you live can create a tax bill.
body_markdown:
You generally don’t have to pay taxes on inheritance money just because you received it. Cash and property inherited from someone generally aren’t federal taxable income. But taxes can arise from inherited retirement accounts, state inheritance taxes or income and gains the assets produce later. Federal estate tax is different because the estate generally pays the tax rather than the beneficiary when it applies.


**A[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sma__falc_relevant&utm_content=doyouhavetopaytaxesoninheritancemoney) can help you manage inherited IRA withdrawals, sales of appreciated property and state-tax exposure with other income to reduce avoidable taxes and plan the timing of taxable events.**


## Is Inheritance Money Taxable at the Federal Level?


The federal government does not impose a separate[inheritance tax](https://smartasset.com/taxes/all-about-the-inheritance-tax) on beneficiaries, and your federal taxable income generally does not include property received by gift, bequest or inheritance. But if that property later generates interest, dividends, rent or other income, those amounts generally become taxable to you. Inherited[traditional IRAs and 401(k)s](https://smartasset.com/retirement/ira-vs-401k) are a major exception, since taxable withdrawals from those accounts are generally taxed as ordinary income.1


Federal estate tax works differently because the IRS taxes the estate itself, and any tax owed is generally paid from the estate’s assets rather than directly by heirs. For someone dying in 2026, the[federal basic exclusion amount](https://smartasset.com/retirement/lifetime-gift-tax-exemption) is $15 million, and the top estate-tax rate is 40%. The table compares how each tax applies:


Tax Who Generally Pays? 2026 Rule Does It Usually Hit the Heir Directly?


Federal inheritance tax Not applicable There is no federal inheritance tax No


Federal estate tax The estate $15 million basic exclusion; top rate of 40% Usually no


Income tax on inherited cash or property Not generally applicable when received Generally excluded from income when received Usually no


Income tax on inherited traditional retirement accounts The heir Taxable withdrawals are generally included in income Yes, when money is withdrawn


Tax on later income The heir Normal income tax rules apply Yes, if the asset later produces taxable income


## States That Tax Inheritances


[State taxes](https://smartasset.com/estate-planning/states-with-no-estate-tax) are where your relationship to the person who died can matter. Kentucky, Maryland, Nebraska, New Jersey and Pennsylvania impose inheritance taxes.2 (Maryland also imposes a separate estate tax.) The table shows how each state treats different heirs:


**State** **Heirs Receiving Exempt or Favored Treatment** **Tax on Other Heirs**


Kentucky3 Spouse, parents, children, grandchildren and siblings generally exempt Class B: 4%–16%; Class C: 6%–16%


Maryland4 Spouse, parents, grandparents, children, lineal descendants, siblings and certain related parties exempt 10%


Nebraska5 Spouse exempt; close relatives generally get $100,000 exemption, then 1% Remote relatives: 11% above $40,000;
others: 15% above $25,000


New Jersey6 Class A, including spouse, parents, children and lineal descendants, exempt Class C: 11%–16% after $25,000 exemption; Class D: 15%–16%


Pennsylvania7 Spouse exempt; transfers from a child age 21 or younger to a parent exempt; lineal heirs taxed at 4.5% Siblings: 12%; most others: 15%


The estate, rather than the beneficiary, pays state estate taxes. Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington impose[estate taxes](https://smartasset.com/taxes/all-about-the-estate-tax) in 2026, as does the District of Columbia. Their exemptions can be far below the federal $15 million amount.

## Taxes on Inherited Investments and Property


Taxable investments and real estate generally receive a[basis adjustment](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/stepped-up-basis) at death. The new basis is usually the asset’s fair market value on the date of death, although alternate valuation and other special rules can apply. When the asset has appreciated, this is commonly called a step-up in basis.


As an example, let’s assume that a parent bought stock for $50,000 and it’s worth $200,000 when they die. The heir later sells it for $210,000, so the taxable gain would generally be $10,000 ($210,000 − $200,000). The $150,000 of appreciation during the parent’s lifetime generally does not become part of the beneficiary’s capital gain under the standard date-of-death basis rule.


The IRS also generally treats inherited capital assets as long-term holdings regardless of how long the[beneficiary](https://smartasset.com/retirement/what-is-a-beneficiary) actually owns them, so any gain is usually taxed at long-term capital gains rates. The table shows how common inherited assets are treated:


**Asset** **General Basis** **When Tax May Apply**


Stocks, ETFs and mutual funds Generally fair market value at death Sale above adjusted basis; later dividends also taxable


Real estate Generally fair market value at death Later gain on sale; rental income


Cash Face value Interest earned after inheritance


## Taxes on Inherited IRAs and 401(k)s


Retirement accounts follow a different set of rules. The IRS taxes withdrawals from inherited[traditional IRAs](https://smartasset.com/retirement/traditional-ira) and pretax 401(k)s as ordinary income. Qualified withdrawals from inherited Roth accounts are generally tax-free once the applicable[five-year requirement is met](https://smartasset.com/retirement/roth-ira-5-year-rule) .


For many non-spouse beneficiaries, the[key deadline is 10 years](https://smartasset.com/taxes/irs-inherited-ira-10-year-rule) . The table shows how the withdrawal rules and tax treatment differ by beneficiary:


**Beneficiary** **General Withdrawal Rule** **Tax Treatment**8


Surviving spouse May have options to keep the account inherited or treat/roll certain accounts into their own Traditional withdrawals generally taxable; qualified Roth withdrawals generally tax-free


Most non-spouse designated beneficiaries Entire account generally must be emptied by Dec. 31 of year 10 Traditional distributions generally ordinary income


Non-spouse beneficiary when owner died after RMDs began Generally annual RMDs during years 1–9 plus full distribution by year 10 Traditional distributions generally[ordinary income](https://smartasset.com/taxes/ordinary-income-vs-capital-gains-tax)


Eligible designated beneficiary May qualify for life-expectancy distributions Depends on account type


A useful distinction is when annual withdrawals are required. If a traditional IRA owner died after their required beginning date, many beneficiaries subject to the 10-year rule must continue annual[required minimum distributions (RMDs)](https://smartasset.com/retirement/all-about-required-minimum-distributions) during the period. If the owner died before the required beginning date, a beneficiary subject only to the 10-year rule generally doesn’t have to take annual distributions before year 10.


Eligible designated beneficiaries can include a surviving spouse, the owner’s minor child, certain disabled or chronically ill individuals and someone who is not more than 10 years younger than the account owner.


How you[time withdrawals](https://smartasset.com/retirement/safe-withdrawal-rate-by-age) within the 10 years can change your tax bill. Say you’re a single filer with $100,000 in other taxable income and you inherit a $300,000 traditional IRA. Withdrawing it all in one year would push most of that money into the 32% and 35% brackets, adding about $92,057 in[federal tax under 2026 brackets](https://smartasset.com/taxes/current-federal-income-tax-brackets) .


Taking $30,000 a year instead would keep each withdrawal in the 22% and 24% brackets, adding about $7,086 in the first year under 2026 brackets. If your other taxable income and the tax brackets stayed the same, that would total about $70,860 over 10 years ($7,086 × 10). The table compares the two approaches:


**Withdrawal Strategy** **Annual Withdrawal** **Additional Federal Tax per Year** **Total Additional Tax**


Lump sum in one year $300,000 $92,057 $92,057


Spread evenly over 10 years $30,000 $7,086 in year one ($5,700 × 22% + $24,300 × 24%) Roughly $70,860 if income and brackets remain unchanged


In this example, spreading withdrawals could save about $21,197 in federal tax under those assumptions.


## Other Inherited Assets and Reporting Rules


Not every inherited asset follows the cash, investment or IRA rules. The table shows how other common assets are taxed and reported:


**Asset** **General Tax Treatment** **Possible Reporting**


Life insurance death benefit9 Generally excluded from income; interest on proceeds is taxable Form 1099-INT may apply


Annuity10 Earnings or other taxable portion may be ordinary income[Form 1099-R](https://smartasset.com/taxes/what-is-a-1099-r-form)


U.S. savings bonds11 Previously untaxed accrued interest may be taxable Form 1099-INT


HSA inherited by spouse12 Generally becomes spouse’s HSA Normal HSA rules


HSA inherited by non-spouse Generally stops being an HSA and becomes taxable to the beneficiary at fair market value[Form 8889](https://smartasset.com/taxes/health-savings-account-tax-form)


Foreign inheritance13 Usually not income merely because inherited, but reporting may apply Form 3520 if threshold exceeded


[Life insurance proceeds](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/how-to-avoid-taxes-on-life-insurance-proceeds) paid because of the insured person’s death are generally tax-free, although interest paid with the proceeds is taxable. U.S. savings bonds may also carry deferred interest that becomes taxable to the estate or beneficiary.


[Health savings accounts (HSAs)](https://smartasset.com/retirement/hsa-vs-401k-2) have a particularly important beneficiary distinction. If the beneficiary is the owner’s spouse, it generally becomes the spouse’s HSA. If someone else inherits it, the account generally stops being an HSA and its fair market value becomes taxable to that beneficiary in the year of death, reduced by certain qualified medical expenses of the deceased owner that the beneficiary pays within one year after death.


A U.S. person who receives more than $100,000 in gifts or bequests from a nonresident alien or foreign estate during the year generally must report the amount on Form 3520, even though the inheritance itself is generally not[taxable income](https://smartasset.com/taxes/what-is-taxable-income) .


## Bottom Line


Inheritance is generally not taxable just because you receive it, but the type of asset, where you live and what happens after the transfer can all create tax consequences. Retirement accounts may trigger ordinary income tax when money is withdrawn, investments and real estate can create taxable gains after a basis adjustment, and some states impose inheritance or estate taxes. Other assets, including HSAs, annuities, savings bonds and foreign inheritances, can have their own reporting rules, so it helps to identify what you inherited before deciding how to manage or use it.
